diagnosis.summary: The pod crashloop-77d8bdc744-6892x is stuck in CrashLoopBackOff because its container exits with code 1 after approximately 2 seconds. The container logs consistently show "FATAL: DATABASE_URL not set", meaning the application requires a DATABASE_URL environment variable (or secret) that has not been configured. The container starts, detects the missing configuration, and immediately exits — causing repeated restarts (38+ observed).

hypotheses.title: Required environment variable DATABASE_URL is not set
hypotheses.mechanism: Every time the container starts, the application logs 'FATAL: DATABASE_URL not set' and exits with code 1 within ~2 seconds (F1, F10). This is a deterministic, repeating failure: the application checks for DATABASE_URL at startup and aborts when it is absent. The missing variable is likely supposed to be injected via a ConfigMap, Secret, or env field in the Deployment spec, but it has not been configured. This causes CrashLoopBackOff with 40+ restarts over ~3.5 hours (F1, F4).

The container lifetime is consistently ~2 seconds and exit code is always 1 (F1). However, the log evidence directly names the missing variable as the sole cause (F10), making this a lower-confidence secondary consideration.

diagnosis.summary: The leakylogger pod (leakylogger-5577459bb8-nb5w6) is in a persistent CrashLoopBackOff. Every time the container starts, it logs several lines (including sensitive credentials in plaintext) and then exits with code 1 on the final line "FATAL: leaked on purpose". The container has restarted 39+ times over ~3.5 hours. The crash is intentional by design of the workload — the app exits fatally on every start. Additionally, the logs reveal the application is leaking secrets (database credentials, AWS keys, authorization tokens, private keys) in plaintext to stdout on every crash cycle.

hypotheses.title: Container exits with code 1 on every start — intentional fatal crash
hypotheses.mechanism: On each restart, the app container prints connection strings, passwords, AWS keys, and authorization tokens in plaintext, then logs 'FATAL: leaked on purpose' and exits with exit_code=1. This is consistent across both the earliest and newest log excerpts (F10), spanning the entire observation window. The CrashLoopBackOff (F1, F4) is a direct consequence of the container never completing startup successfully. The workload appears deliberately designed to crash and leak secrets.

verify.purpose: Confirm the exact fatal error message and secret leakage on the most recent crash cycle
Confirm exit code, restart count, CrashLoopBackOff state, and any additional container status details

diagnosis.summary: The Deployment "stuckrollout" is stuck mid-rollout because its new ReplicaSet (stuckrollout-557464b9d5) cannot pull the image "registry.invalid/app:v2". DNS resolution for "registry.invalid" fails entirely ("no such host"), so the single new pod (gsgn5) is stuck in ImagePullBackOff. Two pods from the previous v1 ReplicaSet (8565fb48dc) are Running and Ready, while the v2 pod has never started a container. The rollout cannot progress past its first new pod.

hypotheses.title: New image registry hostname is unresolvable — registry.invalid/app:v2
hypotheses.mechanism: The Deployment was updated to use image 'registry.invalid/app:v2'. The hostname 'registry.invalid' does not exist in DNS (DNS lookup returns 'no such host'). Every pull attempt by the kubelet on oncall-worker fails with ErrImagePull / ImagePullBackOff. No container has ever started for the new pod (F20, F21). The rollout is blocked: the new ReplicaSet has 1 desired pod that is permanently unready, so the Deployment controller cannot scale down the old ReplicaSet further and the rollout stalls.

verify.purpose: Confirm the rollout is still stuck / not progressing.
Show the full event history and image pull error details for the stuck new pod.

hypotheses.title: oncall-worker2 is cordoned — reduces scheduling capacity during rollout
hypotheses.mechanism: Node oncall-worker2 has the taint 'node.kubernetes.io/unschedulable:NoSchedule' and is marked unschedulable (F13). This means new pods can only land on oncall-worker. While this did not directly cause the image pull failure, it constrains the rollout to a single node and could compound recovery if oncall-worker also becomes unavailable. One new pod (8565fb48dc-v9wgk) was already scheduled to oncall-worker2 before it was cordoned (F32), suggesting the cordon happened mid-rollout.
